ballTurfStiffness.source: Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 7.1 and Table 4(b) (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
ballTurfStiffness.note: Gugan, roll stroke A4R from 8000 frame/s video: "The transient hollow formed in the ground is surprisingly large, about 50 mm in diameter for A4R." and "the downward velocity of the ball can be estimated to be close to 5 m/s immediately after impact, so comparing this with the upward velocity of 2.48 m/s gives a CoR for the ground of about 0.5." Table 4(b) 'Maximum penetration into ground, mm': A2R 4.0, A3R 5.0, A4R 7.2 (upward speeds leaving the ground 1.52, 1.76, 2.48 m/s). The 50 mm chord on a ball of radius 46.04 mm gives 7.38 mm, agreeing with the measured 7.2 mm. Derivation with the impact model's own law (linear spring-dashpot clamped at zero force, damping from e = 0.5, damping ratio 0.2553): the peak penetration at impact speed v is 0.7071·v/ω0 with ω0 = sqrt(k/m), so k = m·(0.7071·v/δmax)² = 0.5·m·v²/δmax² = 0.5 × 0.45359 × 25 / 0.0072² = 1.09e5 N/m (A4R), giving a contact time of 5.5 ms. Bounds: lower 1.0e5 (the same derivation allowing for the hollow already 2.2 mm deep when the mallet releases the ball); upper 2.7e5 from the undamped energy balance k = m·v²/δmax² over A2R to A4R (taking each downward speed as upward speed / 0.5): 2.62e5, 2.25e5, 2.15e5 N/m. Gugan's timing favours the stiffer end: "assuming that the almost linear region after about 5 ms is due to flight". One court only; Gugan: "courts can be expected to vary greatly depending on their composition, their grass covering, and their dampness". Feeds the default lawn's turfStiffness. Since P2b.2b.2b.2a it feeds the head–turf plane law alone; the balls stand on the bed (bedModulus, bedRecovery).

bedModulus.source: Fitted (scripts/turfFit.ts) to Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 7.1 and Table 4(b) (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
bedModulus.note: The turf bed's modulus (P2b.2b.2b.2a design §4.2, §4.4). Two targets, two parameters, with bedRecovery: a free ball meeting a fresh bed vertically at 5 m/s leaves at e 0.5 after a maximum penetration of 7.2 mm (A4R; Gugan: "the downward velocity of the ball can be estimated to be close to 5 m/s immediately after impact, so comparing this with the upward velocity of 2.48 m/s gives a CoR for the ground of about 0.5"). Solved to 1e-4 relative on both; the energy balance at 7.2 mm gives about 3e8 N/m³ for an elastic bed. No bounds: one court only (Gugan: "courts can be expected to vary greatly"); lawn presets and their bounds are P3's.

bedRecovery.source: Fitted (scripts/turfFit.ts) to Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 7.1 and Table 4(b) (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
bedRecovery.note: The turf bed's recovery time τ_r = η/k_w (P2b.2b.2b.2a design §4.2, §4.4), fitted with bedModulus to A4R (see its note). Held out: A2R and A3R's penetrations, 4.0 and 5.0 mm (docs/superpowers/probes/2026-10-09-p2b2b2b2a-turfFit.txt). No bounds (P3).

ballBallContactTime.source: Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 4, Table 1 row 5 (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
ballBallContactTime.note: Table 1 'Ball /ball contact time, Tb, ms' for seven clean scatter shots at ball speeds 1.90-7.64 m/s: 0.75, 0.75, 0.50, 0.75, 0.75, 0.87, 0.75. Gugan: "The ball on ball contact times, Tb, (row 5) show no significant variation with ball speed, and cluster around 0.75 ms (i.e. 6 video frames), close to those for mallet on ball contact times". Resolution is one frame (0.125 ms). Bounds are the table's range. Stan Hall's 1.8 ms (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/hall/) is for balls starting in contact and driven by the mallet, not a free collision.

ballObstacleContactTime.source: Derived from ballBallContactTime (this file): Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', section 4, Table 1 row 5 (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
ballObstacleContactTime.note: No measurement of a ball striking a hoop upright or the peg was found. Oxford Croquet's 'Measuring Hoop Rigidity' (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/rigidity/) proposes methods and reports no data; Rod Cross's high-speed experiments (https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/cross1/) cover ball-ball and mallet-ball contacts only. Derivation (P2b.2a design §4): for the impact's linear law a ball meeting an immovable body has the same natural frequency as two balls meeting, since the ball-ball pair has half the stiffness (two balls in series) and half the effective mass; the analogue value is therefore ballBallContactTime, 0.75 ms. Lower bound: Hertzian contact time scales as (m*^2/(E*^2 R*))^(1/5), and a ball on a rigid body has twice the reduced mass, radius and effective modulus of two equal balls, so T x 2^(-1/5) = 0.87 T; 0.87 x 0.5 ms (the ball-ball lower bound) = 0.435 ms. Upper bound: an upright gives in the turf, which the rigid model omits and no source quantifies; the allowance is 1.0 ms, the largest bound for which the obstacle fuzz keeps every obstacle penetration under its bound (0.06 R), with a margin: 1.0 ms gave 0.055 R, and 1.5 ms (2 x 0.75 ms) gave 0.081 R (P2b.2a pre-flight, 2000 strokes). Every hoop and the peg carries its own contact time (World), so a later version can vary hoop setting stiffness hoop by hoop or by lawn.

faceBallContactTime.source: Stan Hall, 'When a Mallet Strikes a Ball', Table 1 (Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/hall/; Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', Tables 2, 3 and 4(a) (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
faceBallContactTime.note: Hall, electrical timing: "For single ball strokes the contact time is almost constant at 1 ms except for very short distances in which case the time is longer." (Table 1 averages from 7.3 to 2.4 m/s: Dawson 0.89, 1.0, 1.18 ms; Jaques <0.84, 0.94, 1.03 ms; 2.9 ms (Dawson) and 1.32 ms (Jaques) for a 0.6 m stroke). Gugan, high-speed video, 'Duration of contact, Th, ms (± 0.1 ms)': drives 1.00, 0.75, 0.60, 0.60; stop shots 0.75, 0.63, 0.63; rolls 1.13, 1.25, 1.00, 0.88. Value 0.8 ms is the centre of the drive and stop-shot figures; bounds run from Gugan's shortest to Hall's 2.4 m/s average. Gugan notes Hertzian theory predicts shorter contacts for stronger strokes but "the effect is weak"; the linear law here made it speed-independent. Since P2b.2b.2b.2a a check, no longer read by the engine: the face's contact time is faceContactTimeFit (0.8 ms is the fit's value near 2.83 m/s).

faceRestitutionFit.form: 1 - e^2 = a + b * U^p, U the closing speed (m/s)
faceRestitutionFit.source: Don Gugan, 'Inelastic collision and the Hertz theory of impact', Am. J. Phys. 68, 920 (2000), DOI 10.1119/1.1285850, https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan/
faceRestitutionFit.note: Gugan: with K(U) ≡ (1-e^2(U)), "both sets of data can be expressed by K(U) = K0 + K1U^0.4", with K0 and K1 "0.213(5) and 0.077(4) on wood" (the croquet ball on a wooden face; 0.198(2) and 0.112(2) on steel). e falls from 0.854 at 0.5 m/s to 0.793 at 6 m/s, agreeing with Gugan 1 Table I (85.7 % at 0.50 m/s to 79.5 % at 6.01 m/s; mallet.json faceRestitution). The range is that of Gugan's measured e; the engine clamps a closing speed to it (P2b.2b.2b.2a design §3.3).

faceContactTimeFit.form: T = t0 * (U / u0)^q, U the closing speed (m/s)
faceContactTimeFit.source: Don Gugan, 'Inelastic collision and the Hertz theory of impact', Am. J. Phys. 68, 920 (2000), DOI 10.1119/1.1285850, https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan/
faceContactTimeFit.note: Gugan, Table I (the Jaques croquet ball on wood): T 0.97 ms at 2.19 m/s, 0.79 ms at 5.50 m/s. "The data were compared with Hertz's theory using weighted, least-squares, log-log fits. This gave exponents of 0.77 ± 0.03 and -0.23 ± 0.03 for A(U) and T(U), respectively, compared with values of 0.8 and -0.2 given by Eqs. (5)." Only q = -0.23 is Gugan's regression; t0 and u0 anchor on Table I's first row. The fit sits 0.031 ms above the 3.67 m/s row (0.861 ms against 0.83 ms) and 0.023 ms above the 4.24 m/s row (0.833 ms against 0.81 ms), outside Gugan's standard deviation of the times, "± 0.02 ms". Measured over 2.19-5.50 m/s; Hertz predicts U^-0.2. Extrapolated as its power law over the face's range (1.36 ms at 0.5 m/s, 0.77 ms at 6 m/s; P2b.2b.2b.2a design §3.3). Held out: Hall's longer contacts on slow strokes (1.3-2.9 ms on a 0.6 m stroke; faceBallContactTime's note).

tangentialStiffnessRatio.source: L. E. Silbert, D. Ertaş, G. S. Grest, T. C. Halsey, D. Levine, S. J. Plimpton, 'Granular flow down an inclined plane: Bagnold scaling and rheology', Phys. Rev. E 64, 051302 (2001), DOI 10.1103/PhysRevE.64.051302, https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0105071
tangentialStiffnessRatio.note: A discrete-element modelling convention, not a croquet measurement. Silbert et al.: "For Hertzian contacts [37], the ratio kt /kn depends on the Poisson ratio of the material, and is about 2/3 for most materials. For ease in our simulations, we use a value kt /kn =2/7, which makes the period of normal and shear contact oscillations equal to each other for Model L [38]. However, the contact dynamics are not very sensitive to the precise value of this ratio." Bounds are 2/7 and the Hertzian 2/3. The engine's TANGENTIAL_STIFFNESS_RATIO (impact/contactLaw.ts) must equal this value.

handCouplingPeriod.note: Provisional; P2b.2b.2 fits it, with armMass, reachSlack and the grips, to the coaching ratios. The natural period of a firm grip: each hand's gain is k = g·M·(2π/T)² and c = 2ζ·sqrt(k·M), its twist gains alike with the head's inertia about the shaft (design §3.3). It was first to be the shortest period, at damping ratio 0.7, for which the hands' impulse beyond the feed-forward in a 3 m/s centre strike on a single ball stays within 5 % of the ball's momentum change; the one-hand pre-flight search gave 0.077 s (4.98 %), and the user kept 0.08 s (4.80 %). Under the two-hand model that criterion no longer constrains it: from contact the hands track velocity only and the top hand is a pivot on the shaft's line, so the impulse is 0.40 % at 0.08 s and 2.3 % at 0.01 s (two-hand prototype). What keeps the strike the head's is the effective mass the face presents (design §3.4, exit criterion 3). Bounds: the one-hand pre-flight sweep's range (10-200 ms).

handCouplingDampingRatio.note: Provisional; P2b.2b.2 fits it. The damping ratio of a firm grip, for each hand's translation and twist alike (design §3.3). Bounds: the one-hand pre-flight sweep's range (0.2-1).

armMass.source: P2b.2b.1 design §3.3 and §7 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-04-p2b2b1-swing-shot-design.md): the two-hand prototype's calibration (branch proto-two-hands, commit aeadd4c)
armMass.note: Provisional; P2b.2b.2 fits it to the coaching ratios. The effective mass of the player's arms and hands, carried rigidly at the top grip, so that it and the head swing as one body (design §3.3); it adds inertia, not weight, since the arm's weight is the player's. No measurement of an effective arm mass in a croquet stroke was found. With it the swung body presents 1.007 kg at the drive's face centre along aim (design §3.4). Bounds: the range the prototype tried, from 0 (the head alone) to 1.5 kg.

reachSlack.source: P2b.2b.1 design §3.3 and §7 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-04-p2b2b1-swing-shot-design.md): the two-hand prototype's calibration (branch proto-two-hands, commit aeadd4c)
reachSlack.note: Provisional; P2b.2b.2 fits it. The user's release by reach: the bottom hand, on an arm, opens once the shaft's turn since contact carries its grip further than this, (top - bottom)·Δθ > reachSlack (design §3.3). No measurement was found. In the prototype the release opened only in the drive's follow-through, about 110 ms after contact. Bounds: the range the prototype tried (0.01-0.03 m).

headTurfFriction.source: Stan Hall, 'When a Mallet Strikes a Ball', section 'Coefficients of Friction' (1994; Oxford Croquet, updated 28 April 2026), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/hall/
headTurfFriction.note: No measured friction of a mallet head on turf was found. Analogue: Hall slid croquet balls embedded in polystyrene along a croquet court: "For a fairly fast court (normal, cut to 6mm) the coefficient was 0.48. For a fairly heavy court, the coefficient was 0.53." (friction.json ballTurfSliding). A wooden head's base or rim sliding on the same turf is taken alike: 0.5, between the two. Bounds: an allowance for wood against plastic and for a rim against a flat (P2b.2b.1 design §7). P2b.2b.2 sources it, and decides whether a heel ploughing into the turf needs a drag term.

headDeepLimit.source: P2b.2b.1 design §4.2 (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-04-p2b2b1-swing-shot-design.md); upper bound: Don Gugan, 'The Physics of Croquet Strokes: Analysis of the CA high-speed DVD', Table 4(b) (2009; Oxford Croquet), https://oxfordcroquet.org/tech/gugan4/
headDeepLimit.note: A model limit, not a property of turf. The impact's turf is a plane with a linear spring, fitted to a ball pressed into it (ballTurfStiffness); a mallet head's edge or rim presses a footprint that law was not fitted to, so a head driven more than this below the turf plane raises impact-head-deep. Provisional. Upper bound: the deepest ball penetration Gugan measured, 7.2 mm (Table 4(b), roll A4R).

armStiffness.source: Fortineau, Siegler, Makarov and Rodriguez-Ayerbe, 'Human arm endpoint-impedance in rhythmic human-robot interaction exhibits cyclic variations', PLoS One 18(12):e0295640 (2023), DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0295640, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10721195/fullTextXML
armStiffness.note: k₀, the arm's endpoint stiffness at low effort: each hand's flex spring is k_h = k₀ + κ·|F_ff,h| (P2b.2b.2b.2b design §3.1-§3.2). Quoted: "The average estimated stiffness was 116 N/m (SD 60), with a minimum value of 45 N/m and a maximum of 401 N/m" (Experiment H, 31 participants at two target heights), and "endpoint-impedance parameters ranged from 45 to 445 N/m" over both experiments. The rule takes the paper's mean over its 31 participants, which it reports. Bounds: the reported range over both experiments, 45-445 N/m.

armStiffnessPerForce.source: Takagi, Xiong, Kambara and Koike, 'Endpoint stiffness magnitude increases linearly with a stronger power grasp', Sci. Rep. 10:379 (2020), DOI 10.1038/s41598-019-57267-0, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC6962455/fullTextXML
armStiffnessPerForce.note: κ, the endpoint stiffness gained per newton of the hand's force, in N/m per N (design §3.1-§3.2). Analogue: the slope is against the hand's power-grasp force, not the arm's voluntary push. No open figure was found for the slope against the arm's voluntary force: Perreault, Kirsch and Crago (2001, 2002, 2004) report it but are paywalled, and their abstracts give no number. Takagi, Table 1, the major-axis term K yy at the centre posture: "166.9 ± 20.3" N/m at 5 N of grasp to "205.2 ± 27.2" N/m at 20 N, (205.2 - 166.9)/15 = 2.55 N/m per N; the paper: "The endpoint stiffness magnitude increased linearly with the grasp force, and this linear relationship did not depend on the arm's posture". Bounds: K yy's slope over the left (2.48), centre (2.55) and right (2.46) postures and the second experiment's centre (2.56). K xx rises less, 0.23-0.91 N/m per N.

armDampingRatio.source: Derived from Fortineau, Siegler, Makarov and Rodriguez-Ayerbe, PLoS One 18(12):e0295640 (2023), DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0295640, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10721195/fullTextXML, and its S1 Data, https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?type=supplementary&id=10.1371/journal.pone.0295640.s001
armDampingRatio.note: ζ_arm, held constant so that each hand's damper is c_h = 2·ζ_arm·√(k_h·m_arm), as Perreault, Kirsch and Crago (Exp. Brain Res. 157:507, 2004) found the arm's damping ratio "remarkably consistent" across forces and postures (design §3.1-§3.2). No open copy or citing paper quotes their ratio, so it is derived from Fortineau's Experiment H means: "The average estimated damping was 9.9 Ns/m (SD 3.1)", stiffness 116 N/m and mass 0.4465 kg (armStiffness, armEndpointMass); 9.9/(2·√(116·0.4465)) = 0.69. Bounds: B/(2·√(K·M)) over the S1 Data's 62 Experiment H estimations (31 participants at two heights), 0.058-1.42; 12 of them exceed 1.

armHoldStiffness.source: Patel, O'Neill and Artemiadis, 'On the effect of muscular co-contraction on the 3D human arm impedance', IEEE Trans. Biomed. Eng. (2014), DOI 10.1109/TBME.2014.2323938, accepted manuscript https://horc-lab.github.io/pdf/patel2014effect.pdf
armHoldStiffness.note: k_hold, each arm's endpoint stiffness while it holds its posture, the flex's k₀ through the push (gate round 12 ruling, 2026-10-12): k = k_hold + κ·|F_ff| there, κ the grasp-force analogue still on top, since Patel's subjects were coupled at the forearm with no grasp. Four male subjects, seated and strapped, the right forearm coupled near the wrist, 8 mm perturbations in 18 directions over 100 ms, seven 3D configurations, here at 0 % co-contraction. Fig. 1A sets the human-centred frame: X up, Y lateral, Z forward from the subject, so the fore-aft axis, along aim at the grip, is K zz. Table I, 'ARM STIFFNESS CHARACTERISTICS FOR 0% CO-CONTRACTION, AVERAGED ACROSS ALL SUBJECTS', K zz over configurations 1-7: 1353.4, 854.3, 701.1, 504.2, 489.2, 601.2 and 704.3 N/m; the value is their mean, 744.0 N/m, the configurations weighted alike as the paper does not single one out. Bounds: the configurations' means, 489.2-1353.4 N/m. The vertical K xx is 245.2-801.3 N/m (mean 535.3); the flex is isotropic and takes the along-aim axis, which carries the push.

armHoldDamping.source: Tsuji, Morasso, Goto and Ito, 'Human hand impedance characteristics during maintained posture', Biol. Cybern. 72:475-485 (1995), DOI 10.1007/BF00199890, copy http://www.neuro-it.net/pdf_dateien/summer_2004/Tsuij%201995.PDF
armHoldDamping.note: c_hold, each arm's endpoint viscosity while it grasps and holds its posture, the flex's damper through the push (gate round 12 ruling, 2026-10-12), in place of 2·ζ_arm·√(k·m_arm). The abstract: 'hand stiffness and viscosity increase with the grip force of the subject'. Table 4, 'Estimated hand impedance while the subjects grasped the handle in order to keep the hand location', the fore-aft term B yy (y the shoulder-to-hand direction in the horizontal plane) for subjects A and C at hand locations 1-4: 16.85, 30.02, 19.32, 10.84, 27.69, 29.09, 19.91 and 11.93 N·s/m; the value is their mean, 20.71. Bounds: their range, 10.84-30.02. Without grasping (Table 1) the same terms are 5.5-23.0 N·s/m.

armEndpointMass.source: Fortineau, Siegler, Makarov and Rodriguez-Ayerbe, 'Human arm endpoint-impedance in rhythmic human-robot interaction exhibits cyclic variations', PLoS One 18(12):e0295640 (2023), DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0295640, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10721195/fullTextXML
armEndpointMass.note: m_arm, the arm's measured endpoint mass, which sets each hand's damper with ζ_arm (design §3.1-§3.2). Quoted: "The average mass estimated for h 1 * was 459 g (SD 126) and 434 g (SD 94)" (Experiment H; the S1 Data label the second h3*), and "227 to 893 g" over both experiments. The paper gives no single mean, so this is the mean of the two, each over the same 31 participants: (459 + 434)/2 = 446.5 g; the S1 Data's 62 values give 446.8 g. It is the endpoint inertia the robot felt at the hand, not the armMass the swing carries. Bounds: the reported range, 227-893 g.

pendulumForce.source: Hallbeck, 'Flexion and extension forces generated by wrist-dedicated muscles over the range of motion', Appl. Ergon. 25(6):379 (1994), DOI 10.1016/0003-6870(94)90057-4, as tabulated by Napper, Sayal, Holmes and Cudlip, 'Sex differences in wrist strength: a systematic review', PeerJ 11:e16557 (2023), DOI 10.7717/peerj.16557, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10725665/fullTextXML
pendulumForce.note: F_pendulum, the largest forward force the bottom hand applies perpendicular to the shaft by wrist and forearm in the pendulum phase, scaled by pendulumEffort (design §4.2). A measured maximal wrist-flexion force at the hand: Napper et al., Table 3, Hallbeck (1994), 30 males and 30 females, force transducer, isometric (N): males "Average over all postures: 73.15", females "Average over all postures: 55.42", over wrist postures from 90° flexion to 90° extension. Hallbeck's paper is paywalled; the review's table is open. The value is the mean of the two equal groups, (73.15 + 55.42)/2 = 64.3 N. Bounds: the lowest and highest posture means of either sex, females at 75° extension (39.11 N) and males at 90° flexion (104.24 N).

pushForce.source: Das and Wang, 'Isometric Pull-Push Strengths in Workspace: 1. Strength Profiles', Int. J. Occup. Saf. Ergon. (JOSE) 10(1):43-58 (2004), DOI 10.1080/10803548.2004.11076594, https://www.ciop.pl/CIOPPortalWAR/file/8665/2013031212638&das1.pdf
pushForce.note: F_push, the cap on the hands' push intent in carry mode: through the push the hands push along aim with the balls' resistance on the head at the last step, up to F_push (P2b.2b.2b.2b gate ruling 2026-10-11). The largest forward horizontal push a standing adult gives at the hand: Das and Wang measured maximal isometric pushes of 8 men and 8 women, standing, with the preferred arm, level (vertical angle 0°: from the elbow at normal reach, from the shoulder at maximum and extreme reach, so the value's extreme-reach figures are at shoulder height) straight ahead (horizontal angle 90°), in the normal, maximum and extreme reach envelopes. Tables 7 and 8 (N, mean): men 89.39, 77.92 and 106.34; women "660.22" (a misprint for 66.22, its SD 18.48), 48.49 and 78.11. The largest is at extreme reach for both; the value is the mean of the two, (106.34 + 78.11)/2 = 92.2 N. One-handed: no open two-handed standing figure was found, so this caps the two hands' push together with one arm's strength. Bounds: the lowest and highest of those six means, 48.49 (women, maximum reach) and 106.34 N (men, extreme reach).

pushResponseTime.source: Augustsson, Gunhamn and Andersson, 'Relationship Between Early and Maximal Isometric Upper-Body Push and Pull Force Production Among Elite Female and Male Swedish Track and Field Throwers', Sports 13(7):226 (2025), DOI 10.3390/sports13070226, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12300538/fullTextXML
pushResponseTime.note: τ_push, the time constant of the hands' push intent: the sensed resistance follows the balls' resistance as R̃ ← R̃ + (R − R̃)·(1 − exp(−dt/τ_push)) (gate ruling amendment, user, 2026-10-11: primed hands, no reflex delay, the push building at the muscles' pace). A voluntary force rise from force onset, so no reflex or electromechanical delay is in it: Augustsson et al. measured an isometric two-handed bench-press push, 'as quickly and forcefully as possible', in 17 female and 13 male throwers, force onset found as Tillin et al. describe. Table 2, push force as a percentage of peak force at 50, 100, 150, 200 and 250 ms: females 39, 60, 72, 80, 84; males 37, 56, 66, 72, 77. The time to 1 − 1/e (63.2 %) of peak, interpolated linearly between 100 and 150 ms, is 113.4 ms (females) and 136.1 ms (males); the value is their mean, 124.7 ms, rounded to 0.125 s. Bounds: τ = −t/ln(1 − F(t)/F_peak) at each reported time for either sex, 101.2 ms (females, 50 ms) to 170.1 ms (males, 250 ms); the rise is not exactly exponential. Trained throwers; an untrained player is likely slower.

forearmMass.source: Dong, Welcome, McDowell and Wu, 'Modeling of the biodynamic responses distributed at the fingers and palm of the hand in three orthogonal directions', J Sound Vib 332(4):1125–1140 (2013), DOI 10.1016/j.jsv.2012.10.003, PMC4656148, author manuscript https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/36218/cdc_36218_DS1.pdf
forearmMass.note: M0, the effective mass of the wrist and forearm (x_h: 'the effective mass of the wrist and forearm is represented by M0 in the 5-DOF model'). Response-based 0.300, ISO 0.2360. Dong et al. fit a 5-DOF lumped model to the driving-point impedance measured at the fingers and the palm of seven subjects holding a handle (30 N grip, 50 N push, 16–500 Hz) in each of ISO 5349's directions. The x_h direction is taken, normal to the palm: the direction a palm pushes a shaft along aim. The model, as its text describes it: the finger skin M4 and the palm skin M3 move with the handle; M4 joins the fingers M2 through K4, C4; M3 joins the palm–hand dorsum M1 through K3, C3; M2 joins M1 through K2, C2; M1 joins the wrist and forearm M0 through K1, C1; M0 joins the ground (the body) through K0, C0. Value: the mean property-based 5-DOF model, x_h (Table 2), which the paper calls the more reliable; its undamped natural frequencies with the handle held, 26.7, 90.9 and 188.5 Hz, are reproduced by this topology (26.7, 90.8, 188.3 Hz). Bounds: the parameter over the paper's three x_h 5-DOF models, the mean response-based (Table 1), the mean property-based (Table 2) and the proposed ISO 10068 revision's (Table 3). Gate round 3 ruling (user, 2026-10-11, 'Full arm chain'): each hand holding the mallet in carry mode is this chain.
